title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text: Main Functions of the Operating System (review)

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text:
Memory Management
Its goal is to provide safe, isolated, and efficient memory use for every running process.
Typical tasks: Memory allocation: assigning memory to programs and processes during execution. Relocation: mapping a program’s logical addresses to physical memory addresses. Protection mechanisms: preventing a process from accessing another process’s or the OS’s memory. Memory deallocation: releasing and reusing memory that is no longer needed. Address translation: converting logical (virtual) addresses to physical addresses using the MMU. Virtual memory management: extending physical memory with secondary storage so larger programs can run. Efficiency: optimizing memory utilization (page replacement, caching, reducing fragmentation).

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text: Memory Management – Historical Overview

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text:
Fixed Addressing (1950s)
Initially, only one program resided in memory
Programs used fixed addresses Only one program could run at a time To run another program, the current one had to be written to secondary storage (swapping)
Advantage: simple and suitable for batch systems Disadvantage: poor memory utilization and no protection
The program could use the entire physical memory

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text:
Relative Addressing – Static Allocation (early 1960s)
Allowed multiple programs to reside in memory if they fit
When loading programs, the OS added a fixed offset to addresses (programs remained tied to a location) Programs contain relative addresses The actual address is formed from the relative address plus the offset Programs that did not fit in memory waited on secondary storage The OS swapped programs between memory and secondary storage
Advantages: better memory utilization and easier programming Disadvantages: more complex implementation, handling multi-part programs, lack of protection

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text:
Relative Addressing – Dynamic Allocation (mid-1960s)
Base and limit registers were added to hardware, enabling dynamic address translation.
For each memory access, the physical address is the logical address plus the base register. The limit register prevented a program from accessing other processes’ memory. Programs could therefore be relocated during execution Programs received their own address spaces and no longer saw all physical memory Basic memory protection was achieved Address translation became hardware-supported (a predecessor of the MMU – Memory Management Unit)

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text:
Partitioned Systems (early/mid-1960s)
Memory was divided into fixed- or variable-size partitions.
Fixed partitions: simpler, but cause internal fragmentation when a program is smaller than its partition Variable partitions: more flexible, but may cause external fragmentation when gaps remain between partitions The OS became responsible for tracking and managing free memory areas
Physical address = Base address (partition address) + Logical address (offset)
Management techniques: bitmap, linked list Algorithms: first fit, next fit, best fit, worst fit

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text:
Segmentation (around 1970)
A program’s logical units can be organized into separate segments (code, data, stack, etc.).
Each segment has its own base and limit values. Hardware support (segment-table management; segment registers: CS, DS, SS, ES) Permissions can be assigned to segments Segments can be shared Internal fragmentation is eliminated, but external fragmentation remains Can be combined with paging (see next slide)
12.7: Segmentation - Engineering LibreTexts
Logical address = (segment identifier, offset) Physical address = base + offset

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text:
Paging (early 1970s)
Memory and programs are divided into equal-sized pages and frames.
Page sizes were initially 4 KB or 8 KB, later up to 2 MB Permissions can be assigned to pages Goal: eliminate external fragmentation and enable more flexible memory management The program uses a contiguous address space, while pages may be scattered in physical memory Address translation uses a page table, which can become very large
Logical address = [page identifier | offset] Physical address = frame address + offset
Operating System - Memory Management

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text:
Page Tables and Their Implementation
Concept A page table maps virtual addresses to physical addresses. Each process has its own virtual address space. Address translation is performed by the MMU (Memory Management Unit), often accelerated by a TLB. Implementation Single-level page table (per process) Multilevel page table (multilevel index) Hashed page table (lookup using a hash function) Inverted page table (stores information about physical frames in one shared table)
OS - 2.6 (MV) (6) Multi-Level Page Tables
Hashed Page Tables in Operating System - GeeksforGeeks

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text:
Virtual Memory (mid-1970s)
The entire program does not need to be in memory – only currently used pages are loaded. The MMU (Memory Management Unit) performs address translation; the OS manages page replacement From the 1980s onward, the MMU became integrated into the CPU If a page is not in memory, a page fault occurs and the OS loads it from disk. Internal fragmentation may occur The apparent memory can be much larger than physical memory.
9_05_PageTable.jpg (720×699)
Physical address = (frame address × page size) + offset

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text:
Modern Memory Management (from the 1980s)
Combines paging, segmentation, and virtual memory management
Based primarily on paging with fixed-size blocks Address translation is performed by the MMU and accelerated by the TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer) Memory protection is especially important Some pages reside in RAM, while others are on secondary storage (virtual memory) Segmentation has become less important and today mainly appears logically at the programming level Various optimization techniques appeared: Prefetching: loading pages in advance Memory compaction: reducing fragmentation Modern page-replacement algorithms Larger pages to improve TLB efficiency

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text:
Windows 11 – Memory Management
Characteristics Fully paged virtual-memory system Each process has its own address space. Page size: 4 KB (normal), 2 MB / 1 GB (large pages). Paging file (pagefile.sys) Stores infrequently used pages on secondary storage. Copy-on-Write support When a process creates a new instance of itself, the OS does not copy pages immediately; copying occurs only when one instance writes to them. Memory compression (since Windows 10) Separation of kernel and user address spaces – protected kernel memory. Main components Memory Manager (ntoskrnl.exe) Page Frame Number (PFN) Database – tracks RAM pages Working Set Manager – determines which pages remain in RAM Standby and Free Lists – manage available pages

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text:
Linux – Memory Management
Characteristics Full virtual memory; each process has its own 64-bit address space. Demand paging: only pages actually used are loaded. Page size: 4 KB (x86_64); huge pages: 2 MB, 1 GB. Swap partition/file Copy-on-Write mmap (memory mapping): a system call that maps a file or device into a process’s virtual memory Shared memory: fast data exchange between processes without files NUMA support: with multiple CPUs, processes are placed on or near the CPU associated with their memory Transparent Huge Pages (THP): using larger pages when appropriate Components: MMU, TLB – hardware address translation Kernel Memory Manager (mm/) Page Cache – file cache OOM Killer – terminates processes when memory is exhausted

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text:
macOS – Memory Management
Characteristics Mach-based virtual-memory system. Page size: 4 KB Compressed Memory – inactive pages are compressed in RAM. Unified Buffer Cache – shared file and memory cache. Copy-on-Write support Dynamic Pager (swapfile)
Components: MMU, TLB – hardware address translation Kernel Memory Manager (mm/) Page Cache – file cache OOM Killer – terminates processes when memory is exhausted

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text:
Page-Replacement Algorithms
If a new page must be loaded and no free frame remains, the OS must select a page to replace.
Steps: A program accesses a page not in memory (page fault) → page replacement The OS must load the page from secondary storage. If there is no free space in RAM, it must choose which existing page to evict. The new page replaces the selected page. If the page was modified, it must first be written to disk. If it was not modified, it can simply be discarded. Major page-replacement algorithms: FIFO, Optimal, LRU, LFU, Second Chance, NRU

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text:
FIFO Algorithm
Characteristics: Simple queue-based implementation. Advantage: easy to implement, low overhead. Disadvantage: Belady’s anomaly – more memory (frames) does not always reduce page faults.
Example: 3 frames; page-reference string: 7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4,2,3.
Replaces the page that has been in memory the longest.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text:
Optimal Algorithm
Characteristics: Cannot be implemented in real time Can serve as a reference for other algorithms
Example: 3 frames; page-reference string: 7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4,2,3.
Always replaces the page whose next use is farthest in the future (theoretical optimum).
Step-by-step operation

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text:
LRU (Least Recently Used) Algorithm
Characteristics: Assumes that recently used pages are likely to be used again. Used in modified/approximate forms by Linux and Windows A good practical approximation of the optimal algorithm. Disadvantage: more expensive to implement (requires timestamps or a stack).
Replaces the least recently used page.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text:
LFU (Least Frequently Used) Algorithm
Characteristics: Assumes that infrequently used pages are unlikely to be needed later. Disadvantage: aging problem – old pages may remain because of past usage counts. Less commonly used in general-purpose operating systems.
Example: 3 frames; page-reference string: 7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4,2,3.
Removes the least frequently used page.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text:
Second Chance (Clock) Algorithm
Characteristics: If R=1 → reset it and skip the page; If R=0 → replace the page. Fast; approximates LRU. Implementation: circular buffer (clock hand).
Example: 3 frames; page-reference string: 7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4,2,3.
FIFO-based, but each page gets a “second chance” using an R-bit.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text:
NRU (Not Recently Used) Algorithm
Characteristics: Classifies pages into four categories: (1) not referenced, not modified; (2) not referenced, modified; (3) referenced, not modified; (4) referenced, modified. Always selects a page from the lowest available category. Simple, fast approximation of LRU.
Example: 3 frames; page-reference string: 7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4,2,3.
Uses R (referenced) and M (modified) bits.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text: Comparison of Page-Replacement Algorithms

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text:
Page Replacement in Windows
LRU approximation using multiple lists and adaptive page-fault monitoring
Basic principle: an LRU variant using several lists: Active list: recently used pages Standby list: older pages still in memory Modified list: modified pages not yet written out Free/Zeroed list: free or zeroed pages The page-replacement approach can be viewed as combining Clock-Pro/LRU-like ideas. The Windows Working Set Manager manages each process’s working set: removes pages from the working set under memory pressure, can return them if they are needed again. It also monitors page-fault frequency (PFF).

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text:
Page Replacement in Linux
LRU-based, two-list, adaptive page replacement
Basic principle: two-list LRU-style implementation. Active list – recently used pages Inactive list – older pages; replacement candidates are selected here Both may contain: anonymous pages (e.g. heap, stack) page-cache pages (files, mmap, etc.) During page reclaim, pages are evicted from the Inactive list. The kernel uses Clock/Enhanced Second Chance-like techniques: pages have referenced and dirty flags (R/M-like bits), pages move between active and inactive lists over time. Additional modern features: kswapd daemon – monitors memory pressure and reclaims pages in the background, zswap / zram – compressed-memory techniques used before or instead of disk swap. NUMA awareness – preference for process-local, CPU-near memory.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 06
text:
Page Replacement in macOS/iOS
Two-list LRU-style management + memory compression + priority-based memory handling.
In the XNU kernel, page-management logic includes BSD-derived concepts: Inactive queue + Active queue, LRU-style management. In modern macOS: Compressed Memory first tries to compress inactive pages before using disk-backed swap. Memory is managed with process/task priorities in mind (e.g. foreground vs. background work). iOS uses Jetsam/memorystatus mechanisms to terminate low-priority apps under memory pressure.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
What Is Process Scheduling?
Process scheduling is one of the operating system’s most important tasks. The OS decides which process runs, when it runs, and for how long.
Principles: Fairness: every process should get a chance to run. Efficiency: keep the CPU busy. Fast response: interactive processes (e.g. handling keystrokes) should respond quickly. Reduce average turnaround time: complete jobs as quickly as possible. Types (levels) of scheduling: Long-term: which processes are admitted to memory (job scheduling). Medium-term: which processes the OS suspends or resumes. Short-term: which process gets the CPU next (CPU scheduling). I/O scheduling: which process gets access to an I/O device.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
Scheduling Levels
https://www.cs.uic.edu/~jbell/CourseNotes/OperatingSystems/3_Processes.html
Processes are stored in a job queue. Ready processes are placed in a separate ready queue. Processes waiting for I/O are placed in separate I/O waiting queues. Other waiting queues may also exist.
Long-term scheduler Medium-term scheduler Short-term scheduler I/O scheduler

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
Context Switching
Context switching is the process by which the OS saves the state of one process and loads the state of another.
Steps: Interrupt / scheduling event (e.g. time quantum expires, I/O request, higher-priority process). Save the current process state to its PCB (program counter, registers, stack pointer, memory information). The scheduler selects the next process from the ready queue. Load the next process state from its PCB. The CPU resumes execution with the new process.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
Classification of Scheduling Algorithms
Preemptive Scheduling A process can be interrupted before it finishes using the CPU. If a higher-priority process arrives or the time quantum expires, the OS takes the CPU away from the current process. Advantage: better response time; essential for interactive systems. Disadvantage: more context switches and higher overhead. Examples: Round Robin (RR), Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), preemptive priority scheduling. Non-preemptive Scheduling A process cannot be preempted: once it gets the CPU, it runs until it finishes or voluntarily releases it (e.g. for an I/O request). Simpler, with less overhead. Disadvantage: long-running processes can make shorter ones wait → longer turnaround time. Examples: First Come First Served (FCFS), Shortest Job First (SJF), non-preemptive priority scheduling.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
Scheduling Criteria
CPU utilization: keep the CPU working whenever possible. Throughput: number of processes completed per unit of time. Turnaround time: total time from arrival to completion (waiting + execution + I/O). Waiting time: time a process spends in the ready queue waiting for the CPU. Response time: in interactive systems, time from submitting a request to the first response. Fairness: every process should get a chance to run → avoid starvation.

text: Classical Scheduling Algorithms

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
Exercise
Consider six processes with the following characteristics: P1: arrival=0, burst=8, prio=2 P2: arrival=1, burst=3, prio=1 P3: arrival=2, burst=6, prio=3 P4: arrival=5, burst=4, prio=2 P5: arrival=9, burst=2, prio=4 P6: arrival=7, burst=5, prio=1 where “arrival” is the arrival time, “burst” is the required CPU time, and “prio” is the process priority. In what order should the operating system execute the processes?

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
FCFS (First-Come, First-Served)
Characteristics: Non-preemptive algorithm Easy to implement Fair Efficiency can depend heavily on process order. Long processes may delay shorter ones (convoy effect). Poor response time in interactive systems.
Processes receive the CPU in order of arrival.
Applications: batch systems, Windows print queues, Linux I/O queues.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
Example – FCFS
Average turnaround time: (8 + 10 + 15 + 16 + 19 + 19) / 6 = 14.5 Average waiting time: (0 + 7 + 9 + 12 + 14 + 17) / 6 = 9.83 Average response time: (0 + 7 + 9 + 12 + 14 + 17) / 6 = 9.83
Turnaround = Completion − Arrival Waiting = Turnaround − Burst Response = Start − Arrival

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
SJF (Shortest Job First)
Characteristics: Non-preemptive: once a process starts, it runs to completion. Provides the optimal average waiting time. Disadvantage: requires advance knowledge of CPU burst times. Starvation may occur: if short processes keep arriving, long processes may never get CPU time.
A scheduling algorithm that always selects the shortest available process.
Application: Unix/Linux (in modified forms).

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
Example – SJF
Average turnaround time: (8 + 10 + 4 + 12 + 15 + 26) / 6 = 12.50 Average waiting time: (0 + 7 + 2 + 8 + 10 + 20) / 6 = 7.83 Average response time: (0 + 7 + 2 + 8 + 10 + 20) / 6 = 7.83
Turnaround = Completion − Arrival Waiting = Turnaround − Burst Response = Start − Arrival

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
Priority Scheduling (non-preemptive)
Characteristics: Easy to implement. Waiting time may be shorter for high-priority processes. Starvation may occur if low-priority processes are continually postponed. Often used in time-critical systems. Not necessarily optimal in terms of average waiting time.
The scheduler always selects the highest-priority process (e.g. the one with the lowest priority number).
Application: older Unix operating systems.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
Example – Priority Scheduling (non-preemptive)
Average turnaround time: (8 + 10 + 9 + 15 + 24 + 19) / 6 = 14.17 Average waiting time: (0 + 7 + 4 + 11 + 18 + 17) / 6 = 9.50 Average response time: (0 + 7 + 4 + 11 + 18 + 17) / 6 = 9.50
Turnaround = Completion − Arrival Waiting = Turnaround − Burst Response = Start − Arrival

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
Round Robin (RR)
Characteristics: • Fair CPU allocation in interactive systems. • Response time is generally good, but context-switching overhead increases. • The quantum size is critical: too small → many context switches; too large → FCFS-like behaviour.
CPU time is divided into fixed quanta; processes receive CPU time in round-robin order.
Application: modern operating systems (combining time-sharing and priority).

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
Example – Round Robin (q=2)
Average turnaround time: 17.17 Average waiting time: 12.50 Average response time: 3.50
Turnaround = Completion − Arrival Waiting = Turnaround − Burst Response = Start − Arrival

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
SRTF – Shortest Remaining Time First
Characteristics: • Preemptive: a newly arriving shorter process can preempt the current one. • Gives optimal average waiting time if burst times are known. • Long processes may starve if many short processes keep arriving.
The process with the shortest REMAINING CPU time always runs.
Related concept: Linux CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler).

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
Example – SRTF
Average turnaround time: 10.83 Average waiting time: 6.17 Average response time: 1.83
Turnaround = Completion − Arrival Waiting = Turnaround − Burst Response = Start − Arrival

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
Priority Scheduling (preemptive)
Characteristics: • Flexible response to urgent tasks. • Risk of starvation for low-priority processes. • Priority inversion can be handled with protocols (e.g. priority inheritance).
The highest-priority process (lowest priority number) always runs. A newly arriving higher-priority process may preempt the current one.
Application: almost all modern operating systems.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
Example – Priority Scheduling (preemptive)
Average turnaround time: 13.67 Average waiting time: 9.00 Average response time: 7.67
Turnaround = Completion − Arrival Waiting = Turnaround − Burst Response = Start − Arrival

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
Comparison of Algorithms – Summary
FCFS: Simple, but long processes cause the convoy effect. Moderate average times. Priority (non-preemptive): Slightly better, but low-priority processes may starve. Priority (preemptive): Flexible, short response time, but starvation is possible. Round Robin: Good response time in interactive systems, but many context switches → longer turnaround times. SJF: Low waiting and turnaround times, but CPU burst time must be estimated. SRTF: Optimal average times, but long processes may starve.
Important: 1) Operating systems can usually only estimate expected execution time. 2) These are theoretical algorithms; in practice, combinations or modified versions are used.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text: Modern Scheduling Algorithms

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
Multilevel Queue (MLQ)
Characteristics: • Simple but rigid structure. • Combines multiple algorithms. • Each queue may use its own scheduler (e.g. interactive: RR, batch: FCFS). • Processes cannot move between queues.
Applications: • Older operating systems, batch systems.
Multilevel queues: each process is assigned to a predefined queue.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ)
Characteristics: • Dynamically adapts to process behaviour (“learning”). • Interactive tasks respond quickly. • CPU-intensive tasks move to lower-priority queues.
Applications: • Windows scheduler (priority classes), Linux CFS, macOS.
Multilevel queues in which processes can move between queues based on CPU usage.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
Real-Time Scheduling
Characteristics: • Hard real-time: missing a deadline is unacceptable. • Soft real-time: some delay is tolerable. • Meeting deadlines is the primary goal rather than optimizing average times.
Applications: • RTOS (pl. VxWorks, QNX), Linux RT patch, Windows RT.
Scheduling algorithms focused on meeting process deadlines.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
Real-Time Scheduling
Classical algorithms and CFS target good average interactive performance (fair allocation, good response times). Real-time scheduling focuses on guarantees even in the worst case, rather than average performance. Therefore, real-time schedulers use specialized algorithms (RMS, EDF).
Practical applications: Linux: PREEMPT_RT real-time kernel patch for real-time capabilities. Windows also has a real-time priority class, but it is closer to soft real-time (deadlines may occasionally be missed). Embedded systems: automotive controllers, robots, industrial control systems → hard real-time scheduling is common.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
Rate Monotonic Scheduling (RMS)
Characteristics: • Optimized for periodic tasks. • Provably optimal fixed-priority scheduler. • Simple implementation, low overhead.
Applications: • Embedded systems, industrial controllers, real-time operating systems.
Fixed-priority algorithm: shorter period → higher (static) priority.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
Earliest Deadline First (EDF)
Characteristics: • Optimal dynamic method: if a feasible schedule exists, EDF can provide it. • Efficient resource utilization. • More complex implementation, higher overhead.
Applications: • Real-time systems, Linux EDF module, embedded systems.
Dynamic priority: the task with the nearest deadline always runs.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
Scheduling in Multiprocessor Systems
The scheduling algorithms discussed so far were developed for single-processor (single-core) systems. What changes in multiprocessor (multicore) systems?
In multiprocessor systems, the scheduler must manage not only CPU time but also which core executes each process.
Relevant mechanisms: CPU affinity: assigning a process to a specific CPU core → better cache efficiency and fewer migrations.Example: Linux – taskset command. Load balancing: distributing processes evenly across CPU cores → avoids overloaded cores. Example: handled automatically by the Linux kernel.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
Practical Example: Linux CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler)
The default Linux scheduler; it combines ideas from SJF, RR, and priority scheduling.
Characteristics: Fair-share principle: each process receives a proportional share of CPU time; no process can monopolize it. Red-black tree: a balanced data structure enabling efficient lookup and runtime tracking. Nice value: user-adjustable priority (−20 = high, +19 = low).

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
Practical Example: Windows Scheduling
Characteristics:
Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ) principle • Multiple priority queues; processes move dynamically between them. • Interactive tasks receive higher priority.Priority classes • 32 priority levels (0–31), including 16 dynamic levels. • User processes normally run in the Normal class (8–15). Quantum (time slice) • Changes dynamically by process type (shorter for interactive tasks, longer for batch tasks). Example: all Windows 10/11 editions and Windows Server.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 04
text:
Practical Example: macOS Scheduling
Characteristics:
XNU kernel scheduler • Combines the Mach microkernel with BSD scheduling logic. Hybrid MLFQ principle • Multilevel feedback queue + dynamic priority adjustment. QoS (Quality of Service) levels • System processes, interactive tasks, and background tasks receive different levels. • Developers can indicate task importance through an API (also in iOS apps).Example: macOS and iOS scheduling – consistent across the Apple ecosystem.

ARM Processor Architecture
64-bit RISC architecture Manufacturers: Apple, Qualcomm, MediaTek, Ampere, AWS Heterogeneous cores: P-cores (performance) + E-cores (efficiency); dynamic scheduling, DVFS. SoC integration: CPU + GPU + NPU + DSP + ISP + modem on a single chip Ecosystem: Android, iOS, Linux, macOS, Windows on ARM. title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
What Is a CPU Core?
In multicore CPUs, each core has its own ALU, Control Unit (CU), and registers. The cores share main memory and the system bus. The cores share some of their resources. This allows the CPU to execute multiple instructions simultaneously.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
What Is a CPU Thread?
In multithreaded processors, each physical core contains multiple logical processors. Threads share the resources of the core. The operating system treats them as physical processors.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02

Increasing numbers of cores and threads Specialized processing units, e.g. GPUs, TPUs, NPUs Heterogeneous architectures (P/E cores) Improved energy efficiency Smaller process nodes (below 2 nm) New materials, e.g. graphene New technologies, e.g. 3D packaging AI integration (e.g. AI accelerators, encryption)

RAM
The computer’s main memory
Two main types: Static RAM (SRAM) Does not require refreshing Fast but expensive Used as cache memory
•
Dynamic RAM (DRAM)

SIMM modules 1980 – 1998 May contain SRAM and DRAM chips Typical of 80486 and early Pentium systems
DIMM modules (2000–) Used in modern computers Primarily DRAM Higher capacity and performance DDR1–DDR5, with DDR6 coming soon

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
Expansion Cards – ISA Bus
ISA = Industry Standard Architecture
Characteristics: Introduced in 1984 16-bit data bus 8 MHz clock speed Supported cards (main types) Network card Sound card Graphics card Hard disk controller card Successor: EISA (1987)

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
Expansion Cards – VESA Bus
VESA = Video Electronis Standard Association
Characteristics: Introduced in the early 1990s 32-bit data bus 25–100 MHz clock speed Supported cards (main types) Graphics card Network card Hard disk controller card I/O card

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
Expansion Cards – PCI Bus
PCI = Periferial Component Interconnect
Characteristics: Introduced in the early 1990s 32–64-bit data bus 33–66 MHz clock speed Plug and Play support for expansion cards Supports almost all types of expansion cards Versions: PCI 1.0, 2.0–2.3, PCI-X, PCI Express

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
Expansion Cards – AGP Bus
AGP = Accelerated Graphics Port
Characteristics: Introduced in the late 1990s Designed for graphics cards Improved graphics performance Higher speed than PCI Versions: 1x, 2x, 4x, 8x

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
Expansion Cards – PCI Express Bus
The most common expansion bus in modern computers
Characteristics: Introduced in 2003 Serial bus Four main lane configurations; most devices use x4 or x16 Replaces earlier bus standards Versions: 1.0–6.0, with 7.0 coming soon Graphics cards, SSDs, network cards, sound cards, etc.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
Chipset
One or more integrated circuits that manage data flow between the CPU and other motherboard components.
Main functions: Communication hub Memory controller PCI Express lanes System bus Power management Overclocking support Security features

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
BIOS
BIOS = Basic Input/Output System, the interface between the computer’s hardware and software.
Main functions POST (Power On Self Test) Initializing hardware components Selecting the boot device Defining the boot order Loading the operating system CMOS settings Security features Firmware update Handling hardware interrupts

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
CMOS
CMOS = Complementary Metal-Oxide Semiconductor, a small memory used to store BIOS settings.
Main functions Storing system settings (even when the computer is powered off) Communication with the BIOS Implementation Usually NVRAM (Non-Volatile RAM)

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
CMOS Setup Utility
A utility for configuring BIOS settings
Some important functions: Basic and advanced settings Hardware information and status Security settings Power management Restoring default (factory) settings

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
BIOS vs UEFI
UEFI = Unified Extensible Firmware Interface, the modern successor to BIOS.
Image source
Near future: BIOS gradually disappearing Automatic updates More modern user interface
Advanced security features

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
TPM
TPM = Trusted Platform Module
A dedicated motherboard chip that provides security functions. Key storage Disk encryption Secure Boot Password protection Secure updates Windows 11 requires TPM 2.0.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
Power Supply Connectors
Provide power to the motherboard, processor, fans, and some peripherals.
Power connector types: AT (older computers, ribbon-style connector) ATX (Advanced Technology Extended), 20/24-pin – motherboard power EPS (Extended Power Supply), 4+4 or 8+8-pin – CPU power PCIe – power for graphics cards and high-power expansion cards SATA 15-pin – primarily powers storage devices Molex (older computers, 4-pin)

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
Motherboard Cooling
Main motherboard components requiring cooling: CPU → dedicated cooler (fan + heatsink, or liquid cooling). VRM (Voltage Regulator Module) → heatsinks around the CPU to maintain stable power delivery. Chipset → often actively cooled in older systems; usually a passive heatsink today. M.2 SSDs → often use dedicated heatsinks because they can run hot at high speeds.
Cooling solutions: Passive cooling → aluminium heatsinks (chipset, VRM). Active cooling → small fan (older chipsets, high-end motherboards). Additional cooling → liquid-cooling blocks on premium motherboards.
CPU fan
heatsink

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
Fan Connectors
Older types Molex (4-pin peripheral connector) Powered directly from the PSU (typically 12 V). No speed control. Now obsolete; used with older case fans.
Modern motherboard connectors 3-pin fan connector (DC) 1: ground, 2: +12 V, 3: tachometer (speed feedback). Controlled by voltage regulation. 4-pin fan connector (PWM) 1: ground, 2: +12 V, 3: tachometer, 4: PWM control signal. More precise speed control and quieter operation. Current standard for CPU and case fans.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
Storage Connectors
Enable communication between the computer and storage devices.
Main types IDE (Integrated Drive Electronics) SCSI (Small Computer System Interface) SATA (Serial Advanced Technology Attachment) RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) M.2, U.2 PCIe

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
Secondary Storage
Storage devices can hold large amounts of data and retain their contents when the computer is powered off.
Common storage devices Hard disk drive (HDD) CD, DVD, Blu-ray SSD USB flash drive

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
Optical Storage – CD, DVD, Blu-ray
Optical storage media in which information is encoded in the physical structure of the disc.
Image source
Light reflects differently from pits (indentations) and lands (surface)
Typical interfaces: IDE, SATA, SCSI, USB

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
Optical Storage – Advantages and Disadvantages
Advantages Archiving and storing movies Capacity up to 100 GB (Blu-ray XL) Redundant data storage Potentially long lifespan Disadvantages Slow (CD: 150 KB/s – Blu-ray: 216 MB/s) Obsolete – many computers no longer include optical drives Prone to physical damage Future Declining use However: new technologies, e.g. holographic data storage

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
Secondary Storage – Hard Disk Drives (HDDs)
Magnetic storage devices in which information is stored in a magnetic layer.
Image source
Typical interfaces: IDE, SATA, SCSI

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
HDD – Advantages and Disadvantages
Advantages High capacity (up to 24 TB) Low-cost storage Reliable for long-term storage Multiple interfaces: IDE, SCSI, SATA, SAS Disadvantages Slow (150–300 MB/s) Sensitive to physical shock Moving parts Future Servers and data centres (low cost, high capacity) New technologies, e.g. laser-assisted writing and reading Capacity expected to reach 30–40 TB

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
Secondary Storage – SSDs
An SSD (Solid State Drive) is an internal storage device based on NAND flash memory.
NAND flash memory Memory cells are arranged in a grid
A memory cell can store one or more bits (SLC – Single-Level Cell, MLC, TLC, QLC) Cells contain one or more floating-gate transistors
The state of the memory cell is determined by the presence or absence of charge on the floating gate.
Typical interfaces: SATA, M.2, U.2, PCIe

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
SSD – Advantages and Disadvantages
Advantages Significantly faster data transfer than HDDs No moving parts Lower power consumption Compact size, multiple form factors Multiple interfaces/protocols: SATA, PCIe, NVMe, etc. Disadvantages Higher cost Limited write endurance Future Higher speeds (PCIe) and capacities (up to 100 TB), with broader adoption

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
Data Storage – What to Expect
Emergence of new memory technologies Memristor – fast, durable, non-volatile memory bridging RAM and secondary storage Phase-change memory (PCM) – stores 0 and 1 using phase changes in a material STT-MRAM (Spin-Transfer Torque Magnetic RAM) – magnetic, energy-efficient, durable memory ReRAM (Resistive RAM) – data storage based on changes in electrical resistance
Increasing data density HAMR (Heat-Assisted Magnetic Recording) and MAMR (Microwave-Assisted Magnetic Recording) for HDDs Holographic storage – 3D laser-based storage with theoretical TB–PB capacities
New theoretical directions Quantum data storage – using quantum bits (qubits) DNA data storage – storing data in biological molecules at extremely high density and with long lifespan
Usage trends Growth of cloud storage – supplementing or replacing local physical storage Edge storage – handling data closer to its source (IoT, smart devices)

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
USB Flash Drive
A USB (Universal Serial Bus) flash drive is an external storage device based on NAND flash memory.
Characteristics Portable storage Connects to a USB port Typical capacity: 32–512 GB Typical transfer speed: Limited write endurance
USB Connector Types
Latest USB Standards
A USB-C port can support USB 2.0–USB4, Thunderbolt 3/4, and DisplayPort.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
Thunderbolt 3 and 4
A high-speed universal interface using the USB-C connector.
Supported devices External storage External graphics cards External network adapters Monitors Docking stations, etc.
Characteristics High data transfer speed Compatibility with USB-C devices Combined functions (data, video, power)
Thunderbolt 3 vs. 4: What’s The Difference? (iboysoft.com)

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
Monitor Connectors
VGA (Video Graphics Array, D-Sub, analogue) Introduced in 1987; the PC monitor standard for decades. Analogue signal only; practical high-quality limit around Full HD. Now obsolete, but still occasionally found on projectors.
DVI (Digital Visual Interface, digital/analogue) Introduced in 1999 as the digital successor to VGA. Variants: DVI-D (digital), DVI-A (analogue), DVI-I (combined). Max. 1920×1200 (Single Link) or 2560×1600 (Dual Link). Also being phased out.
HDMI (High-Definition Multimedia Interface) Introduced in 2003, primarily for TVs and home entertainment devices. Digital video + audio over a single cable. Still widely used today, including on monitors and laptops. Versions include HDMI 1.4 (Full HD/4K), HDMI 2.0 (4K 60 Hz), HDMI 2.1 (8K, 120 Hz).
DisplayPort (see later) + others (Mini DisplayPort, USB-C, Thunderbolt)

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
HDMI (High-Definition Multimedia Interface)
Primarily used to transmit audio and video between computers and monitors.
Characteristics: Introduced: 2003 Signal: digital video + audio over one cable + additional data Main uses: TVs, monitors, game consoles, home cinema
Main versions HDMI 1.4 (2009) → 4K @ 30 Hz HDMI 2.0 (2013) → 4K @ 60 Hz HDMI 2.1 (2017) → 8K @ 60 Hz or 4K @ 120 Hz (gaming, VRR, eARC) HDMI 2.2 (2025) → 16K @ 60 Hz, 12K @ 120 Hz, 4K @ 240 Hz; new Ultra96 cable required
Advantages Widely adopted and compatible Standard connector for TVs and consoles
Disadvantages Less flexible than DisplayPort for monitors (fewer displays over one cable) Shorter supported cable lengths at high resolutions

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
DisplayPort
Primarily used to transmit audio and video between computers and monitors.
Characteristics Supports video signals up to 16K resolution Daisy-chaining displays Sharp, high-contrast image High bandwidth (up to 77 Gb/s) Multiple connector formats (standard, Mini DisplayPort, USB-C)
Multiple versions (1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 2.0) Backward compatible with HDMI, DVI, and VGA via adapters

I/O Connectors
Allow external peripherals to be connected to the computer.
Older / disappearing: PS/2, VGA, serial/parallel ports Current basics: USB-A (2.0 / 3.x), LAN (RJ-45), audio jack Modern: USB-C, HDMI/DisplayPort, optical audio, Wi-Fi antenna Premium: multiple LAN ports, 2.5G/10G Ethernet, Thunderbolt 3/4 (USB-C connector)

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 02
text:
Jumpers
Jumpers are small plastic caps containing a U-shaped conductor. They connect or disconnect two pins, allowing switching between two fixed hardware settings.
Modern motherboards have few jumpers; typical uses include: CPU configuration (e.g. clock speed, voltage) Chipset configuration (e.g. bus speed) Boot configuration (e.g. boot order) CMOS reset PnP

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 01

Computer
Computer  Calculator
A computer is a device capable of storing data and sequences of operations (programs) defined by humans and executing them automatically
In a broader sense, the following devices can also be considered computers: Game consoles (Xbox, PlayStation) Embedded systems (mobile phones, smart devices, engine control electronics, GPS, etc.) some IoT* devices

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 01
text:
Embedded systems
Special-purpose computers designed to perform a specific task
They do not look like computers from the outside They are usually small, but can also be large (e.g. traffic-light controllers) Their architecture usually includes: Central processing unit Sensors Output/communication interface Actuators (convert signals, e.g. into motion)

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 01
text:
IoT – Internet of Things
Devices equipped with computing capability and network connectivity
This also includes “smart” embedded systems.
Characteristics: Utility Intelligence Dynamic nature Heterogeneity Security?

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 01
text:
Components of a computer
Three main functional components: processor, memory and I/O unit

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 01
text:
The bus system
A set of communication lines connecting the functional components of a computer. Types: Control bus Address bus Data bus

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 01
text:
Von Neumann principles
Stored-program concept (data and instructions are stored in the same memory in the same way) Sequential instruction execution A fully electronic machine operating with the binary number system Functional units: separate input/output unit, control and processing unit, and memory General-purpose applicability

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 01
text:
The von Neumann architecture problem
The main problem of the architecture is that the processor often has to wait for memory operations, so most of its processing time is unused (“von Neumann bottleneck”)
Other architectures also exist, e.g.: Harvard architecture Parallel architectures

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 01
text:
Harvard architecture
Separate data and instruction memory Greater security Better performance More complex design Applications: Microcontrollers CPUs

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 01
text:
Parallel architecture
Processing multiple data items and/or instructions simultaneously Higher performance Several models More difficult to program

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 01
text:
Parallel architecture – example
UMA – Uniform Memory Access The processors share memory equally Either all processors have equal access to peripherals (symmetric multiprocessing) or only certain processors do (asymmetric multiprocessing)

text:

Quantum computers
Challenges: Sensitive even to very small disturbances As the number of qubits increases, error detection and correction become increasingly difficult They require new algorithms and software

The processor (CPU – Central Processing Unit)
The central processing unit of the computer interprets and executes instructions Components: Control Unit Arithmetic Logic Unit Registers

The Control Unit (CU)
The part of the processor that
Controls data flow between the ALU and the registers Interprets instructions Converts instructions into control signals

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 01
text:
The machine instruction cycle
Fetch: read the address of the next instruction from the PC register Decode: decode the instruction stored in the IR Execute: the CPU passes the required information to the ALU, which executes the instruction
Image source: https://computersciencewiki.org/index.php/The_machine_ instruction_cycle

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 01
text:
The Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU)
Performs arithmetic and logical operations.
Basic operations: Boolean operations Binary addition Complement operation Bit shifting right/left
Image source

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 01
text:
Registers
Small, very fast storage locations Typically 8, 16, 32 or 64 bits wide Usually implemented as static storage They can store
Data: AX, BX, CX, DX Memory addresses: SI, DI, SP, BP, CS, DS, SS, ES, IR Status and control
information: PC, IR, flags

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 01
text:
CISC and RISC processors
CISC Complex instruction set
Compound instructions One instruction – multiple clock cycles
One register set Longer execution time
RISC Reduced instruction set
Simple instructions One instruction – one clock cycle
Multiple register sets Shorter execution time
CISC = Complex Instruction Set Computers RISC = Reduced Instruction Set Computers

Main memory
Stores programs currently being executed and the data they require Random access (RAM – Random Access Memory) The processor can access and address it directly Its contents are lost when power is turned off Usually dynamic RAM (DRAM) – requires refreshing

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 01
text:
Ports
A PORT is a computer interface used to communicate with peripheral devices. It provides a standardized connection between the CPU and peripherals via the system bus (external bus).

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 01
text:
Serial and parallel data transmission
When data is transferred between the peripheral interface and the peripheral one bit at a time, sequentially, this is called serial data transmission. (e.g. mouse, modem) When groups of bits are transferred simultaneously between the peripheral interface and the peripheral, this is called parallel data transmission (e.g. printer). Historical Overview – Fifth Generation
Today’s operating systems Parallel and distributed systems → clusters, grid computing, shared resource management across multiple computers. Network and Internet integration → networking (e.g. TCP/IP) is a core part of the OS. Mobile and embedded operating systems → Android, iOS, RTOS solutions. Virtualization and containers → multiple virtual machines and containers on one physical system. Security and access control → encryption, sandboxing, permission management. Intelligent, self-adaptive operation → AI-based resource optimization, power management, predictive scheduling. title: IT Architecture – Lecture 03
text:
What Is an Operating System?
An operating system is a collection of programs that manages computer resources and interacts with users.
Hardware provides the computer’s physical resources (CPU, memory, secondary storage, network, peripherals). The operating system controls and manages these resources and provides a secure, consistent environment for running programs. Applications access hardware through the operating system, so they do not need to communicate directly with physical devices.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 03
text:
Typical Functions of Operating Systems
Process management and scheduling – controlling running programs and enabling multitasking. Memory management – allocating memory to programs and protecting against invalid access. File-system management – managing files and directories and providing access to them. I/O device management – handling keyboards, monitors, printers, network adapters, etc. User interface – providing a command-line or graphical environment. Protection and security – access control and permission management.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 03
text:
Optional Functions of Operating Systems
Network services – communication protocols and network connectivity. Virtual-machine and container management – isolated execution environments. User and workgroup management – for example, on server systems. Built-in applications and utilities – e.g. text editors and media players. Power management – especially on mobile devices. Special security features – encryption, firewall, antivirus protection.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 03
text:
Classification of Operating Systems – Classical Categories
Mainframe operating systems – run on mainframes and manage very large resources (e.g. IBM z/OS). Server operating systems – provide network services to many clients (e.g. Windows Server, Linux server distributions). Multiprocessor operating systems – run on multi-CPU or multicore systems and are optimized for parallel processing. Personal-computer operating systems – desktop and laptop systems with user-friendly interfaces (e.g. Windows 11, macOS, desktop Linux). Handheld-device operating systems – mobile phones, PDAs, tablets (e.g. Android, iOS). Embedded operating systems – specialized hardware (e.g. cars, routers, IoT devices; often Linux variants or an RTOS). Sensor-network operating systems – for small, resource-constrained sensors (e.g. TinyOS, Contiki). Real-time operating systems (RTOS) – provide guaranteed response times in industrial, military, or medical systems (e.g. VxWorks, QNX).

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 03
text:
Classification of Operating Systems – New Categories
Cloud-oriented operating systems Foundation for virtual machines and services Examples: ChromeOS, Azure Sphere, AWS Firecracker Container-focused operating systems Minimal systems optimized for running containers Examples: CoreOS, RancherOS, k3OS Edge/IoT-specific operating systems For small, resource-constrained devices Examples: RIOT OS, Zephyr, TinyOS

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 03
text:
Operating Systems – The Role of Unix
Adaptable Unix was originally developed in the 1960s–70s at AT&T Bell Labs. It was small, portable, and modular → easy to adapt to different hardware. As a result, it spread rapidly in universities and research environments.
Standard-setting. Unix introduced concepts still used today: file-system hierarchy (/usr, /bin, etc.), the “everything is a file” principle (files can represent devices, processes, text), pipes, processes, and permissions. Unix formed the basis of the POSIX standard → it still shapes Linux, macOS, and many other operating systems.
A common ancestor. Many modern operating systems descend from Unix or Unix-like systems: Linux (a Unix-like system in the free/open-source tradition). BSD systems (FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD; later forming part of the basis of macOS). Android is also based on the Linux kernel. This is why Unix is often called a “common ancestor” → its philosophy remains present in many modern operating systems, even when the code is different.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 03
text:
Basic Concepts – Process
A process is a program in execution. It includes the program code, data, and execution state.
Each process has an address space, registers, open files, and resources The OS records process states in the process table Scheduling: the OS can suspend and resume a process Process tree: parent and child processes, cooperation, and IPC (Interprocess Communication) Signals: handling asynchronous events (e.g. timer, error) Each process is associated with a user (UID, GID)
Process tree

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 03
text:
Process States
Possible states: New – the process is being created. Ready – the process is ready to run and waiting for CPU time. Running – the process is currently executing on the CPU. Waiting / Blocked – the process cannot run because it is waiting for an event (e.g. completion of an I/O operation). Terminated – the process has finished and the OS releases its resources.
Special states: Suspended / Stopped – the process is not running but can be resumed. Zombie – the process has finished, but its parent has not yet collected its status → an entry remains in the process table. Orphan – the parent has terminated, but the child process continues running

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 03
text: Process states

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 03
text:
Basic Concepts – Process Control Block
The Process Control Block (PCB) is an OS data structure containing all information required to manage a process.
Contents Identifiers: PID (Process ID), user ID (UID), group ID (GID) State: current process state (Running, Ready, Waiting, …) Registers: saved program counter, stack pointer, and CPU registers Memory information: address space, page or segment tables Files and resources: list of open files, I/O connections Scheduling data: priority, CPU time, quotas
Role The OS uses PCBs to track and manage processes. If the scheduler suspends a process, the PCB stores its complete state → execution can later resume exactly where it stopped.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 03
text:
Basic Concepts – Threads
A thread is an execution unit within a process.
Threads share the process resources (address space, files). Each thread has its own program counter, stack, and registers The operating system provides thread management and scheduling. Types: kernel threads – managed by the OS; user threads – implemented by libraries rather than directly by the OS Relationship: process = resources + threads that execute the program. Threads are lighter-weight than processes (faster context switching). Concurrency: multiple threads can run within one process (e.g. in a browser, one thread downloads while another renders). Efficient on multicore processors: threads can execute truly in parallel.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 03
text:
Basic Concepts – Address Spaces
An address space is the range of memory a process can use.
It consists of addresses ranging from 0 to a maximum value. It determines which memory a process can access Address spaces prevent processes from accessing each other’s memory (isolation, protection) An address space contains: program code (instructions), program data (variables, global data), the stack (function calls, local variables). Modern applications: sandboxing, virtualization, containers

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 03
text:
Basic Concepts – Files
A file is a named unit of data maintained by the operating system for persistent storage and management.
It may contain text, binary data, program code, images, video, etc. It exists within a namespace (file system, directories). Files have metadata (size, creation time, permissions). The OS provides access → read, write, delete, append.
Modern applications: Files may be network-based (NFS, SMB) or distributed/object-based (HDFS, Amazon S3) Non-file-system storage also exists (e.g. NoSQL databases, object stores).

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 03
text:
Basic Concepts – Input/Output
I/O is the OS subsystem that manages input and output devices. It includes device-independent mechanisms and device-specific drivers.
Device-independent I/O The OS provides general mechanisms that apply to all devices. Example: abstractions for opening files and reading/writing. Device-dependent I/O Handled by device drivers → each hardware device requires a specific driver. Example: printer or graphics-card driver.
Modern applications: Plug & Play, virtual I/O in cloud VMs

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 03
text:
Basic Concepts – Protection
The operating system is responsible for keeping data (e.g. emails, business plans, tax returns) protected and confidential.
Goal: process and data isolation, permission management User and group identifiers (UID, GID) control access Superuser / Administrator with special privileges
Modern applications: With Zero Trust, the OS must continuously verify who is running each process or establishing each network connection and whether access to the resource is authorized Hardware security (TPM, SGX): the OS provides the appropriate interface

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 03
text:
Basic Concepts – Shell
Shell = command interpreter, an interface between the user and the operating system.
A system program that uses OS services. Its role is to accept and execute commands (launch programs, invoke system calls). Supports I/O redirection (> and <), pipes (|), and background processes (&) A GUI serves a similar role → a user interface to the OS. The shell is often used alongside the GUI
Modern applications: Automation and scripting (DevOps and cloud workflows) Managing cloud resources

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 03
text:
Basic Concepts – Kernel
Kernel = the core of the operating system; it directly manages hardware and provides resources to applications.
Main functions (largely the core functions of the operating system) Process management – creating, scheduling, and terminating processes Memory management – virtual memory, address spaces, isolation File system – managing data and metadata I/O management – device drivers and abstracted hardware access Protection and permissions – access control Modern applications: Monolithic kernel – all functions in one large unit (e.g. Linux) Microkernel – minimal kernel; many services run in user space (e.g. MINIX, QNX) Hybrid kernel – combines both approaches (e.g. Windows, macOS XNU)

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 03
text:
Kernel Types
Monolithic kernel All major services (process management, memory management, I/O, file system, drivers) are part of the kernel. Fast → all functions are directly accessible. Disadvantage: large and complex; faults can affect the whole system. Microkernel The kernel contains only essential functions (process management, messaging, minimal memory management); other services (file system, drivers, networking) run as separate user-space processes. Advantage: modularity, stability, easier debugging. Disadvantage: messaging overhead can reduce performance. Hybrid kernel A middle ground: conceptually microkernel-based, but many services run in kernel mode for performance. Attempts to combine stability and speed. Nanokernel An extremely small kernel → mainly interrupt handling and only minimal functionality. Example: some embedded systems. Exokernel (experimental approach) The OS kernel provides direct access to hardware rather than high-level abstractions → applications build their own abstractions. Highly flexible, but complex for developers. Example: MIT Exokernel project.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 03
text:
Operating-System Architectures
Classical: Monolithic system – everything runs in one large kernel (e.g. early UNIX). Layered system – a well-structured OS divided into layers (e.g. THE system). Virtual machine – hardware virtualization allowing multiple independent operating systems (e.g. IBM VM/370). Exokernel – minimal kernel for resource allocation; abstractions implemented in user space (MIT project). Microkernel – only core functions in the kernel; other services in user space (e.g. MINIX 3, QNX).
Modern: Hybrid kernel – microkernel principles, but many modules run in kernel mode for performance (e.g. Windows NT, macOS). Container-based isolation – an OS feature (Linux namespaces, cgroups), used in modern virtualization. Cloud/distributed OS – managing resources across a cluster or cloud (e.g. Kubernetes as a “cluster OS”).

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 03
text:
Basic Concepts – System Calls
A user program cannot access hardware directly; instead, it asks the OS to perform operations through system calls.
Main areas: process management, file management, I/O, memory, communication and protection. Role Security: the kernel checks whether the call is authorized. Abstraction: the program does not need to know hardware details. Consistent interface: all programs access OS functions in the same way.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 03
text:
Basic Concepts – User Mode and Kernel Mode
User mode User programs run in user mode. Restricted access: programs cannot directly access hardware, memory, or I/O devices. For privileged operations (e.g. opening files, memory management, networking), the program uses a system call handled by the kernel. Goal: protection → faulty or malicious programs cannot crash the entire system. Kernel mode (supervisor / privileged mode) The kernel and device drivers run here. Full access to hardware, memory, and CPU instructions. This is where the core of the operating system runs. When control enters kernel mode, the OS has full privileges.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 03
text:
Example – Windows 11 Architecture
Hybrid kernel Neither purely microkernel nor purely monolithic. Originally based on microkernel principles (NT design), but many components remained in kernel mode for performance → hence the hybrid design. Main characteristics Kernel mode: NT kernel, device drivers, memory management, scheduler. User mode: Win32 subsystem, UWP, former POSIX compatibility, .NET CLR. Subsystems: Windows provides multiple APIs for compatibility. Security model: ACLs, UAC, sandboxing, and mandatory TPM 2.0 hardware support in Windows 11. Examples of architecture layers User space: graphical interface (Explorer, UWP apps), system programs. Kernel space: hybrid NT kernel, HAL (Hardware Abstraction Layer), drivers.

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 03
text:
Example – Linux Architecture
Characteristics Monolithic kernel, but dynamically extensible through kernel modules. User space and kernel space are clearly separated. Device drivers and file systems are part of the kernel and can be loaded as modules. Hardware abstraction (device drivers, architecture-specific code). Supports containers (namespaces, cgroups) and virtual machines (KVM).

title: IT Architecture – Lecture 03
text:
Example – macOS Architecture
Characteristics UNIX-based (POSIX-compatible, built partly on BSD). Hybrid kernel: XNU (X is Not Unix). Microkernel elements: Mach (process management, IPC, memory). Monolithic elements: BSD (file system, networking, security). I/O Kit: object-oriented driver model.
